title: The metallic model
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Chemistry (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-30-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: S2.3#c04 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; S2.3#c03 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; S2.3#c06 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; S2.3#c01 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Electrical conductivity of metals
items.clue: Mobile delocalized charge carriers move through the solid.

items.label: Lattice of cations
items.clue: The regular, repeating arrangement of positive ions in a solid.

items.label: Malleability of metals
items.clue: The ability to be hammered or rolled into a new shape without breaking.

items.label: Metallic bond
items.clue: The electrostatic attraction between positive ions and a sea of delocalized electrons.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a metallic bond?

options.text: The sharing of electron pairs between each metal atom and its nearest neighbours
The electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons
The attraction between cations and anions formed by electron transfer between metal atoms
The London forces acting between the closely packed atoms of a metal lattice

questions.explanation: This is the metallic bond as the IB defines it. Each atom releases its valence electrons into a delocalized system shared by the whole lattice, and the resulting cations are attracted to these electrons in all directions.

questions.stem: The melting points of three period 3 metals are sodium 97.8 °C, magnesium 650 °C and aluminium 660 °C. Which statement explains why the melting point increases from sodium to aluminium?

options.text: The relative atomic mass rises, so the heavier atoms need more energy to separate.
Each atom forms more covalent bonds to its neighbours: one for Na, two for Mg and three for Al.
The cations have a higher charge and a smaller radius, so the metallic bonding is stronger.
The London forces between the atoms become stronger as the number of electrons in each atom rises.

questions.stem: Which statement about a piece of solid sodium is correct?

options.text: It carries a positive charge, because its atoms have lost their outer electrons.
It contains no ions; its lattice is made only of neutral sodium atoms.
It is neutral, with one delocalized electron for each Na⁺ ion in its lattice.
Its atoms are joined in pairs, each pair held together by a shared electron pair.

questions.explanation: Each sodium atom releases its one valence electron into the delocalized system, leaving Na⁺. The electrons stay in the metal, so their total charge balances the total charge of the cations and the piece of sodium is neutral.

questions.stem: The melting points of the group 1 metals decrease down the group: lithium 180.5 °C, sodium 97.8 °C, potassium 63.4 °C. Which statement explains this trend?

options.text: Reactivity increases down the group, so the bonds break more easily when the metal is heated.
The cation radius increases, so the delocalized electrons are attracted less strongly.
Larger atoms form longer and weaker covalent bonds with each of their neighbouring atoms.
The cations and anions in the lattice get larger, so their ionic attraction weakens.

questions.stem: Copper is used for the wires in household electrical cables because it conducts electricity very well. What carries the electric current through a copper wire?

options.text: The copper's delocalized electrons, drifting through the lattice
Copper cations, moving through the lattice towards the negative terminal
Electrons from the power supply; the copper's own electrons stay in place
Vibrating copper ions, each passing the energy on to the next ion along

questions.explanation: The delocalized electrons are mobile charge carriers already present throughout the copper. When a potential difference is applied they drift through the lattice of cations, which stay in place. This high electrical conductivity is why copper is used for wiring.

questions.stem: Data for three metals are shown as (A_r; cation; cation radius; melting point): lithium (6.94; Li⁺; 76 pm; 180.5 °C), sodium (22.99; Na⁺; 102 pm; 97.8 °C), calcium (40.08; Ca²⁺; 100 pm; 842 °C). Which statement explains these data using the metallic model?

options.text: Melting point rises with A_r: calcium has the heaviest atoms and the highest melting point.
Calcium is less reactive than sodium, so its bonds are harder to break on heating.
Cation radius decides bond strength: the smallest ion, Li⁺, should give the strongest bonding.
Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ are almost the same size, so the higher charge of Ca²⁺ gives calcium much stronger bonding.

questions.stem: Aluminium is used for heat sinks, which carry thermal energy away from computer processors. Which statement explains why aluminium is suitable?

options.text: Its high melting point lets it absorb all the heat without melting.
Its vibrating ions pass the energy on; its electrons play no part.
Metals stay colder than their surroundings, so it keeps drawing heat away.
Its delocalized electrons carry kinetic energy rapidly through the whole metal.

questions.explanation: A heat sink must conduct energy away quickly. In aluminium the delocalized electrons gain kinetic energy near the hot processor and move rapidly through the lattice, transferring the energy to the cooler fins. This high thermal conductivity is the reason for the choice.

questions.stem: Aluminium is rolled into kitchen foil less than 0.02 mm thick without cracking. Which statement explains this property of aluminium?

options.text: Its layers of cations slide, staying attracted to the delocalized electrons around them.
Its metallic bonds are weak, so the rollers can easily push its atoms apart.
Its bonds between neighbouring atoms bend like hinges instead of breaking.
Its individual atoms are soft, so each one is flattened as it passes between the rollers.

questions.explanation: This is malleability. Because the metallic bond is non-directional, the delocalized electrons keep attracting the cations after the layers have slid into new positions, so the bonding is not broken and the metal changes shape without cracking.

questions.stem: Calcium ([Ar] 4s²) melts at 842 °C. Titanium ([Ar] 3d² 4s²), the next metal but one in period 4, melts at 1670 °C. Which statement explains the higher melting point of titanium?

options.text: Its atoms are heavier than calcium atoms, so more energy is needed to separate them.
Its extra 3d electrons give stronger London forces between its atoms than calcium's have.
Its 3d as well as its 4s electrons are delocalized, so the electron density is higher.
Its 3d electrons are not delocalized, so its smaller cation is what makes the bonding stronger.

questions.stem: Iron ([Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²) is a transition element. Which statement explains the electrical conductivity of solid iron?

options.text: Its 4s electrons are delocalized, but its 3d electrons are core electrons fixed on the cations.
Its cations move through the lattice towards the negative terminal, carrying the charge.
Electrons from the power supply pass through it while its own electrons stay in place.
Its 3d and 4s electrons are delocalized and drift when a potential difference is applied.

questions.explanation: In a transition element the 3d electrons, as well as the 4s electrons, are delocalized in the metallic lattice. These mobile electrons drift through the lattice of cations when a potential difference is applied, carrying the current.
